new_statements.quote: 139. Il ne semble pas exister en mandingue de tons musicaux analogues à ceux que l'on rencontre dans nombre de langues négro-africaines [...] 140. Par ailleurs, il existe en mandingue un accent tonique, un accent de durée et des accents d'intonation émotive ou logique. a) Accent tonique. 141. L'accent tonique, caractérisé en mandingue par la hauteur plus que par l'intensité, et très peu marqué en général, tombe comme en français sur la dernière syllabe du mot. 142. Si l'on a affaire à un mot composé ou dérivé, ou à un groupe de mots formant corps, il se répète sur la dernière syllabe de chacun des composants, mais se fait surtout sentir sur la dernière syllabe du dernier composant.
new_statements.translation: 139. There do not seem to exist in Manding musical tones like those found in many Negro-African languages [...] 140. On the other hand, Manding has a tonic accent, an accent of duration and accents of emotive or logical intonation. a) Tonic accent. 141. The tonic accent, characterized in Manding by pitch more than by intensity, and in general very weakly marked, falls as in French on the last syllable of the word. 142. In a compound or derived word, or a group of words forming a unit, it is repeated on the last syllable of each component, but is felt above all on the last syllable of the last component.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Delafosse supplies a placement (final syllable, pitch-based) for the Manding cluster as a whole (Malinké, Bambara, Dioula), not for Dioula specifically. His denial of tone is contradicted by works 2-4, which treat these varieties as two-tone languages.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (mainly pitch, weak) on the final syllable of every word; in compounds and phrases each component's final syllable carries it, the last component's most strongly; placement is 'absolutely regular' so it is not marked in texts or dictionary (§146); independent of vowel length (§143). The book explicitly denies lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §142: in compounds/derivatives and word groups the accent recurs on the final syllable of each component, with the strongest on the final syllable of the last component (a weaker accent on non-final components).
new_statements.exceptions: None for the tonic accent (§146: placement absolutely regular). A separate lexical 'accent de durée' (vowel length) is unpredictable on monosyllabic roots (§149) and never falls on the second syllable of a native disyllabic root except in loans (§150).
new_statements.identity_note: Braconnier 1990 describes the Dioula of Odienné (north-west Côte d'Ivoire). Coulibaly 1990 describes 'jula' without naming a locality. Diarra 1992 describes Fuladugukakan (Sebekoro, Fuladugu region, Mali), which the author calls very close to standard Bambara; it is not Dioula. Delafosse 1929 treats 'mandingue' as one language (Malinké, Bambara, Dioula) and states the accent rule for the whole cluster. Sangaré 1983 (not opened) concerns the Kong variety.

new_statements.quote: INC prend une valeur tonale inverse de celle du ton auquel il fait suite. Le dioula d'Odienné est une langue à deux tons phonologiques (voir Braconnier (1983a et b)): INC sera donc formé d'un ton haut après ton bas et d'un ton bas après ton haut. C'est ce que nous exprimons en disant que INC est un morphème "à polarité tonale".
new_statements.translation: INC takes a tonal value opposite to that of the tone it follows. Dioula of Odienné is a language with two phonological tones (see Braconnier 1983a and b): INC will thus consist of a high tone after a low tone and a low tone after a high tone. This is what we express by saying that INC is a morpheme 'with tonal polarity'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jula words carry lexical tone patterns (tonemes H and B plus a modulated tone) constrained by a rising L-before-H sequence rule; in level-toned disyllables the second syllable tends to be pitched higher; isolated monosyllables lengthen. No mention of accent, stress or intensity; the greater 'articulatory energy' discussed concerns word-initial versus intervocalic consonants, not syllable prominence.

new_statements.translation: Since this disagreement lies at the level of tonal realisations, we briefly set out our conception of the tonology of the Jula of Kong. [...] 1. In Kong Jula there is no moneme of two or more syllables with an entirely low underlying tone pattern; only a few monosyllabic items have a genuinely low underlying tone, almost all low-toned monosyllables being analysed as carrying an underlying floating high tone that can surface through raising properties (cf. law 2). 2. A progressive tonal assimilation law raises low tones

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Dioula/Jula as tonal (Diallo 2001); Sangaré 1983 describes the Kong (Côte d'Ivoire) variety as a two-tone system with downstep and floating tones and says nothing about stress, consistent with the on-file Braconnier 1990 and Coulibaly 1990 statements (tone language, no stress statement). It neither supports nor addresses Delafosse 1929's weak final 'accent tonique'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kong Jula is analysed with two tones (haut/bas) plus floating high tones, downstep ('abaissement du ton haut') and five realisation laws (no all-low polysyllabic monemes; progressive raising of lows; weakening of the first high after a low; optional shortening of underlying long vowels incl. the low-toned definite lengthening; final nasality). The whole note is tonal and morphotonological (predicative markers lò'/té/bé/kà/-rà etc.); the words accent, accentuation, stress, intensité never occur: no statement about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal only: 'seuls quelques items monosyllabiques ont un ton sous-jacent effectivement bas' (law 1); the accompli suffix -rà is low-toned in Kong unlike Bambara (p. 95); high-toned predicatives have a falling-tone variant whose conditions are unresolved (p. 97).
new_statements.identity_note: Sangaré 1983 describes the 'parler de Kong' / 'jula de Kong' (Kong, north-eastern Côte d'Ivoire), an Ivorian Jula variety under dyul1238, contrasted throughout with standard Bambara and with M.J. Derive's notations of Ivorian Manding predicatives. Braconnier 1983 (unopened) treats the Dioula of Odienné (parler de Samatiguila; Glottolog also lists woje1238 for that area).

tone_statements.quote: Le dioula est une langue à tons : cela signifie que deux mots qui sont écrits avec les mêmes consonnes et voyelles peuvent être différenciés par la hauteur mélodique à laquelle ils sont prononcés. Le dioula connaît deux tons : un ton haut, noté par un accent aigu par exemple (á), et un ton bas noté avec un accent grave, par exemple (à). … sòo «cheval» sóo «maison» … Les noms (substantifs) définis se caractérisent par le fait qu'ils comportent toujours un ton complexe sur la dernière syllabe (par exemple [â, î, ê, ô, û]).
tone_statements.translation: Dioula is a tone language: this means that two words written with the same consonants and vowels can be distinguished by the pitch at which they are pronounced. Dioula has two tones: a high tone, written with an acute accent e.g. (á), and a low tone written with a grave accent, e.g. (à). … sòo 'horse' sóo 'house' … Definite nouns are characterised by always carrying a complex tone on the last syllable (e.g. [â, î, ê, ô, û]).
tone_statements.locator: unpaginated web page, section '3. Les tons' (minimal pairs and definite-noun examples)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high and low, distinguishing words (sòo 'horse' vs sóo 'house'); definite nouns carry a 'complex' tone (written â, ô etc.) on the last syllable. Orthography guide; nothing on word stress.

readall_conflicts: Delafosse 1929 (pp. 104-105) denies that Manding has 'musical tones' and posits a weak, pitch-based 'accent tonique' fixed on the final syllable of every word ('comme en français'); every later work opened treats these varieties as two-tone languages (Braconnier 1990 for Dioula d'Odienné, 'langue à deux tons phonologiques'; Coulibaly 1990 for jula, tonemes with an L-before-H sequence rule; Diarra 1992 for the Bambara-like Fuladugukakan), and none of them mentions word stress at all. Delafosse's final 'accent' is best read as an early impression of the frequent final high tone in Manding words, superseded by the tonal descriptions; no modern source assigns Dioula a word stress.

sources.quote: Le dioula est une langue à tons : cela signifie que deux mots qui sont écrits avec les mêmes consonnes et voyelles peuvent être différenciés par la hauteur mélodique à laquelle ils sont prononcés. Le dioula connaît deux tons : un ton haut, noté par un accent aigu par exemple (á), et un ton bas noté avec un accent grave, par exemple (à). … sòo «cheval» sóo «maison» … Les noms (substantifs) définis se caractérisent par le fait qu'ils comportent toujours un ton complexe sur la dernière syllabe (par exemple [â, î, ê, ô, û]).

tone.translation: Dioula is a tone language: this means that two words written with the same consonants and vowels can be distinguished by the pitch at which they are pronounced. Dioula has two tones: a high tone, written with an acute accent e.g. (á), and a low tone written with a grave accent, e.g. (à). … sòo 'horse' sóo 'house' … Definite nouns are characterised by always carrying a complex tone on the last syllable (e.g. [â, î, ê, ô, û]).
tone.summary: Two tones, high and low, distinguishing words (sòo 'horse' vs sóo 'house'); definite nouns carry a 'complex' tone (written â, ô etc.) on the last syllable. Orthography guide; nothing on word stress.
